record.paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
record.original_question: How much do unresolved multiplicity and post-interaction binaries distort the inferred properties of massive stars and the interpretation of massive-star populations? A complete answer must determine when objects that appear single from photometry or spectral-type calibrations are actually binary-evolution products such as stripped stars or helium-burning O stars, and how such hidden systems bias stellar temperatures, masses, evolutionary states, and population-synthesis conclusions.

evidence.quote: Within clusters or in the field, resolving and understanding the multiplicity of massive stars is crucial to avoid misinterpretations and solution degeneracities. This requires to go beyond photometry-based studies and ideally multi-epoch spectroscopy to quanitatively analyse the components.

The inferred values from photometry or spectral-type calibrations change drastically when presumably single objects turn out to be post-interaction binaries, implying that our interpretations of less-studied objects can be significantly blurred. The examples further show that long-predicted binary-evolution products (e.g., intermediate-mass stripped stars, He-burning O stars) actually “hide” in what one might consider the “known” OB population.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a population of massive OB-type stars whose physical parameters (effective temperature $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$, luminosity $L$, current mass $M$, surface abundances, and evolutionary state) are inferred from observational diagnostics. Two classes of diagnostics are available: (i) broadband photometry combined with spectral-type calibrations applied under the assumption that each resolved source is a single star, and (ii) multi-epoch, quantitative spectroscopic disentangling that can identify and characterize individual binary components. A subset of the population consists of post-mass-transfer binary-evolution products — in particular intermediate-mass stripped helium stars and core-helium-burning O stars — whose composite light and spectra can mimic those of an apparently single OB star.

Quantify, as rigorously as possible, the systematic biases introduced into single-star parameter inference and into population-synthesis conclusions when an unknown fraction $f$ of the apparently single sources are in fact unresolved multiples or post-interaction systems. Specifically:

1. Provide criteria (photometric, spectroscopic, kinematic, or temporal) that allow one to decide, for a given source classified as single, whether it is in fact a binary-evolution product such as a stripped star or a helium-burning O star.
2. Determine the resulting biases in the inferred $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$, $M$, age, and evolutionary classification of individual sources as functions of mass ratio, orbital configuration, and evolutionary phase of the hidden companion.
3. Propagate these biases to population-level statistics (initial mass function, mass-to-light ratio, ionizing photon production, supernova progenitor channels, binary fraction) and quantify the distortion of population-synthesis predictions when hidden post-interaction products are not modeled.

A complete solution should yield quantitative correction factors or a probabilistic framework relating observed (apparent-single) population statistics to the true underlying mixed single-plus-binary population.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broad, ongoing research question in massive-star astrophysics. Recent observational programs (e.g., BLOeM, XShootU, ULLYSES) and theoretical work on stripped stars and post-interaction binaries continue to refine, but have not closed, the quantitative assessment of how hidden multiplicity biases massive-star parameters and population synthesis. The problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
status_evidence.snippet: Resolving and understanding the multiplicity of massive stars is crucial to avoid misinterpretations; long-predicted binary-evolution products hide in the known OB population.
status_evidence.claim: The community treats unresolved multiplicity and hidden post-interaction products as an unresolved source of systematic error in massive-star inference.
